ai.summary: Russia-linked espionage group Cold Relic used a cloud compromise and stolen Google Workspace data to launch linked intrusions, including a 2026 breach at a U.S. organization, according to Google's Mandiant and GTIG.

items.title: Microsoft’s Agent Framework PyPI package compromised to steal credentials

ai.summary: Attackers published two malicious versions of Microsoft's agent-framework Python package, which run a credential stealer every time Python starts. Several security firms reported it.

items.title: Java4Shell Flaw (CVE-2026-114938) Enables Pre-Auth RCE in Jira, Jenkins, Keycloak and More

ai.summary: Oracle plans to release patches on November 17, 2026, for 11 Java SE flaws that may be exploited remotely without authentication. Separate reports warn of a critical OpenJDK remote code execution flaw, with a maximum CVSS 3.1 score of 8.1.

items.title: Researchers Claim Two RCE Exploits That Bypass Telegram’s New Android Defenses

ai.summary: Researchers at NebuSec say a malicious bot widget can get past Telegram's new Android security filter and run code outside it. They demonstrated this on a Telegram test server.

items.title: British Scattered Spider hacker sentenced to 6 years in prison

ai.summary: A leader of the Scattered Spider cybercrime group received a six-year US prison sentence for cryptocurrency theft and plotting to hack about a dozen companies.

items.title: CISA Urges Immediate Patching of Java4Shell Flaw That Could Allow Remote Code Execution

ai.summary: CISA urged prompt patching of CVE-2026-114938, a critical Oracle Java out-of-bounds write flaw that can cause denial of service or remote code execution under certain conditions.

items.title: Microsoft announces Windows Server 2028 with hardened security

ai.summary: Microsoft announced Windows Server 2028, its next server operating system, with hardened security features, at the Ignite 2026 conference. No threat activity is reported.

items.title: Quality Isn’t The Main Worry About AI Pentesting — Data Privacy and Production Safety Are

ai.summary: Article arguing that data privacy and production safety matter more than output quality when choosing AI penetration testing, as AI speeds up both development and attacks.

items.title: Dizigom illegal streaming service with 21M monthly visits shuts down

ai.summary: The Alliance for Creativity and Entertainment announced the shutdown of Dizigom, a large Turkish illegal streaming site, after a settlement with its operators.

items.title: AI Pentesting Checklist for Web Apps: 15 Questions to Ask Before Choosing a Vendor

ai.summary: Checklist of fifteen questions for evaluating AI penetration testing vendors for web applications, noting that exploitation often starts before patches exist.

items.title: New Attack Bypasses TPM Lockout to Crack Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs in Days, Not Years

ai.summary: Researchers showed that opening a PC case lets someone reset the TPM lockout on some AMD and Intel machines, enabling guessing of short Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs.

items.title: Cyberattack hits Norwegian energy giant Equinor, disrupting internal services

ai.summary: Norwegian energy company Equinor is containing a cyberattack on its IT systems that disrupted internal services but has not affected oil and gas production.

items.title: Ice hockey governing body website defaced amid dispute over Russia's exclusion

ai.summary: The International Ice Hockey Federation confirmed hackers defaced its website, replacing the homepage with a pro-Russian message protesting Russia's exclusion from competitions.

items.title: New EggStreme Malware Variant Goes Silent to Evade Security Tools in Government Attacks

ai.summary: A suspected Chinese APT group rebuilt the EggStreme malware to evade security tools while continuing to target Philippine government organisations, according to Bitdefender.

items.title: British hacker gets 6 year sentence for $11.6M crypto theft scheme

ai.summary: Tyler Robert Buchanan, described as the suspected ringleader of a hacking collective, was sentenced to six years for a $11.6M cryptocurrency theft scheme.

items.title: From Deepfakes to Helpdesk Impersonation: Why Stronger Verification Matters

ai.summary: Attackers use deepfakes, helpdesk impersonation and fake IT support requests to trick employees into granting unauthorized corporate system access. Specops urges stronger identity verification to counter these social engineering threats.

items.title: Russian cyber-espionage group used stolen cloud data to hack into organizations, Google says

ai.summary: Russian state-backed hackers are using data stolen from cloud accounts to impersonate trusted contacts and launch espionage attacks on people in victims' professional networks.

items.title: NSA continues response to interruptions in classified internal network

ai.summary: On day two of disruptions to the NSA's classified internal network, staggered arrivals and logins occurred at Fort Meade. A source said classified national security work continued unimpeded.

items.title: N-able Patches 17 N-central Flaws as Attackers Exploit Earlier Bugs to Deploy Crypto Miners

ai.summary: N-able issued N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 3, fixing 17 security flaws, as attackers exploit earlier N-central bugs to install cryptocurrency miners on the RMM and UEM platform.

items.title: ConnectWise Warns ScreenConnect Attacks Continue as SCKit Targets Unpatched Systems

ai.summary: ConnectWise finished probing unauthorized access to partner ScreenConnect environments and urged customers to upgrade. Attacks on on-premises systems with third-party extensions enabled continue, including via SCKit.

items.title: Hijacked Optimizely Scripts Served Card Skimmer and iOS Exploit Kits to CNN, BBC and Zoom Visitors

ai.summary: An attacker exploited a flaw in Optimizely Web Experimentation to inject malicious code into scripts that customer sites load. Visitors to at least 178 organisations, including CNN, BBC and Zoom, were exposed.

items.title: Apple Tightens macOS App Permissions to Limit Data Access Amid AI Agent Security Risks

ai.summary: Apple previewed macOS 27.3 beta 2 controls giving Mac users finer-grained control over app access to data, including for AI agent apps. The changes cover Device Control, Data Access and Full Disk Access.

items.title: Microsoft testing Remote Lock for lost or stolen Windows devices

ai.summary: Microsoft is testing a feature that lets enterprise administrators remotely lock lost or stolen Windows devices without erasing their data.

items.title: New GitDoor and GraphDoor Backdoors Turn GitHub and SharePoint Into Covert C2 Channels

ai.summary: Operation ShadowCloud, reported by Kaspersky, targets government sectors in Asia and Africa using previously undocumented backdoors that abuse SharePoint and GitHub for command-and-control.

items.title: Siemens ROS#

ai.summary: Siemens ROS# before 2.3.1 has a code injection flaw where a crafted message definition file could inject arbitrary code into the generated program. A fixed version is available.

items.title: Dorsett Controls InfoScan

ai.summary: Five vulnerabilities in Dorsett Controls InfoScan could let attackers obtain system information, access application data, recover stored credentials, or intercept and manipulate network traffic.

items.title: Siemens Mendix Studio Pro

ai.summary: Multiple vulnerabilities in the MCP Server of Siemens Mendix Studio Pro could let a network-adjacent attacker access data, run tools, or compromise systems. Siemens released fixed versions.

items.title: Siemens .NET Client Library for SIMATIC S7 Webserver API

ai.summary: Multiple vulnerabilities in Siemens' .NET client library for the SIMATIC S7 Webserver API could expose sensitive information or allow files to be written outside the download directory. A fixed version is available.

items.title: Critical Java Vulnerability Requires Immediate Patching

ai.summary: CISA urges immediate patching of a critical Oracle Java flaw, CVE-2026-114938 ("Java4Shell"), in the Base64 decoder of the JVM. It can crash the JVM and allow unauthenticated remote code execution.

items.title: Siemens Simcenter Femap

ai.summary: An out-of-bounds read in Siemens Simcenter Femap, triggered by opening X_T files, could let an attacker crash the application or execute arbitrary code. A fixed version is available.

items.title: Siemens SIMATIC

ai.summary: Siemens SIMATIC products contain an authentication bypass that lets an on-path attacker hijack a user's session and run code with the victim's privileges. Fixes are being prepared, with interim mitigations recommended.

items.title: Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808

ai.summary: Siemens' RUGGEDCOM APE1808 is affected by a double free flaw inherited from a FortiOS vulnerability disclosed by Fortinet. Siemens advises updating the related Fortinet firewall software.

items.title: Siemens meta-iot2050

ai.summary: A command injection flaw in the firmware update tool of Siemens meta-iot2050 lets an attacker who can manipulate a configuration file run arbitrary commands as root. Fixes are being prepared, with mitigations advised.

items.title: Researchers Detail iPhone Flaw That Let Apps Record Audio Despite Denied Microphone Permission

ai.summary: A now-patched Apple audio service flaw let iPhone and iPad apps record audio even after users denied microphone permission. No exploitation in attacks has been reported.

items.title: Hackers Found a Way Around GitHub SHA Pinning. This Webinar Explains How to Close the Gap

ai.summary: Attackers have bypassed GitHub Actions SHA pinning. In March 2026, hijackers of the Trivy security scanner planted malicious code disguised as GitHub's official checkout tool.

items.title: Inside Modern Phishing Kits Built to Steal Microsoft 365 Sessions

ai.summary: Huntress researchers describe three phishing kits that capture and replay Microsoft 365 session tokens, and how defenders can detect and contain them. Microsoft 365 users are the target.

items.title: Trigram Campaign Impersonates About 50 AI and Blockchain Brands to Target Devs with Infostealers

ai.summary: A campaign called Trigram impersonates about 50 AI and blockchain brands to trick developers into running an infostealer. Stormshield reports that AI, blockchain and logistics sectors in Europe and the US are targeted.

items.title: Flipper Devices launches $399 ‘Flipper One’ Linux-based multi-tool

ai.summary: Flipper Devices, maker of the Flipper Zero pentesting device, launched a crowdfunding campaign for Flipper One, a $399 portable Linux computer and networking multi-tool. No security incident is described.

items.title: Tor releases emergency update amid ongoing DDoS attack

ai.summary: The Tor Project released an emergency update to its relay software to defend against an ongoing DDoS attack. The attack has overwhelmed relays and affected most relay operators.

items.title: Researchers hijack Hugging Face account for popular Kokoro AI model

ai.summary: Researchers gained control of the Kokoro text-to-speech model's Hugging Face account because the platform lacked ownership verification. The model is used in projects from Google, NVIDIA, AMD, Intel and AWS.

items.title: Apple reports outages affecting iCloud Mail, AppleCare and more

ai.summary: Apple reports service disruptions affecting iCloud Mail, iCloud account sign-in, Apple School Manager, Schoolwork and other services. Users of these services are affected.

items.title: Japan takes Fugaku supercomputer offlline after cyberattack

ai.summary: Japan's RIKEN Center for Computational Science took its Fugaku supercomputer offline after a security breach. Details in the text are limited.

items.title: Cloud keys leaked in Docker Hub images are stolen within seconds

ai.summary: Credentials and access secrets exposed in public Docker Hub images are extracted and exploited within about eight seconds of publication, according to the report.

items.title: Critical Java4Shell flaw allows RCE attacks on major Java applications

ai.summary: A critical flaw called Java4Shell in OpenJDK lets unauthenticated attackers run code remotely on enterprise applications including Jenkins, Jira, Confluence and Keycloak.

items.title: BO Team Exploits Log4Shell in VMware vCenter, Compromises Russian Firm's Code-Signing Server

ai.summary: A threat actor exploited Log4Shell in VMware vCenter and spent months inside a Russian software developer's network. It compromised the firm's code-signing server, which Kaspersky ICS CERT investigated.

items.title: Amazon Uncovers AI Agent Campaign Targeting LiteLLM, Dify, and Other Apps for API Keys

ai.summary: Amazon's threat intelligence team found attacker AI agents scanning exposed AI apps like LiteLLM, One API, and Dify. The agents steal provider API keys and use them to run their own searches.

items.title: SANSAR Linux Cryptomining Malware Uses Modified NVIDIA Library to Hide GPU Activity

ai.summary: Threat cluster REF3364 runs a financially motivated Linux cryptomining operation. Its SANSAR toolkit, which uses Tor for commands, tampers with GPU readings to hide mining activity.

items.title: Retadup Worm Resurfaces 7 Years After Takedown to Spread CoffeeLoader Malware

ai.summary: A new CoffeeLoader variant, delivered by Retadup, resurfaced seven years after takedown. An NSIS installer drops a patched 7z.dll and runs it via rundll32.exe, according to Kaspersky.

items.title: Six Unpatched Danfoss Refrigeration Controller Flaws Could Allow Remote Takeover Without Login

ai.summary: Six unpatched flaws in Danfoss AK-SM800A refrigeration controllers could let a remote attacker take over devices without logging in. No patch exists, and the newest firmware does not fix them.

items.title: Google Finds Hackers Using AI Agents to Build and Run Exploits From Software Patches

ai.summary: Google reports threat actors using autonomous multi-agent AI frameworks to build and run exploits from software patches. These frameworks support faster multi-stage intrusions.

groups.name: thegentlemen
groups.about: The Gentlemen is a ransomware-as-a-service group that emerged in July–August 2025 and quickly claimed over 320 victims in 17+ countries. It offers affiliates a 90% revenue share and uses a Go-based locker against Windows, Linux, NAS, and BSD. A 2026 compromised C2 server revealed over 1,570 linked victims.

groups.name: qilin
groups.about: Qilin ransomware was first observed in July 2022. It is written in Golang and offers multiple encryption modes that the operator controls. The group uses double extortion, demanding payment for a decryptor and for not releasing stolen data.

groups.name: incransom
groups.about: INC Ransom is a prolific ransomware-as-a-service operation active since July 2023. It targets healthcare, government, education, and manufacturing in North America and Europe, with no sector excluded. It posted over 200 victims in 2025 alone.

groups.name: akira
groups.about: Akira reportedly emerged in March 2023 and has been speculated to have ties to the former Conti group. Its affiliates reportedly also work with Snatch and BlackByte. The first version was written in C++ and later versions in Rust. Initial access has involved brute-force attacks on Cisco VPNs and exploitation of two CVEs.

groups.name: silentransomgroup
groups.about: Silentransomgroup is described in the notes as a former Conti team, also tracked as Chatty Spider and UNC3753. The notes give no further details on its operations or targets.

groups.name: braincipher
groups.about: Brain Cipher emerged in July 2024 with both Windows and Linux variants. It reportedly uses a leaked LockBit Black build and is suspected of exploiting CVE-2023-28252. Demands start at $150,000 and are paid in Monero. In 2025 it moved its negotiation portal to a new server.

groups.name: rhysida
groups.about: Rhysida is a ransomware-as-a-service group that emerged in May 2023. It uses phishing and Cobalt Strike to breach networks and deploy its payload. It threatens to publish stolen data, leaves PDF notes, and accepts Bitcoin. The notes say the ransomware is still in early development.

groups.name: medusalocker
groups.about: The notes describe Medusa as a DDoS bot written in .NET 2.0, not a ransomware group. Its current command-and-control uses HTTP, while its predecessor used IRC. The notes do not describe ransomware activity, so this entry may be mislabeled.

groups.name: safepay
groups.about: SafePay emerged in September 2024 and grew rapidly while rejecting the RaaS model, running all operations in-house. It claimed over 300 victims worldwide by mid-2025. An early high-profile attack on UK telematics firm Microlise reportedly stole 1.2 TB of data.

groups.name: play
groups.about: Play ransomware, also called PlayCrypt, was first observed in June 2022 and uses double extortion. It has targeted many organizations in Latin America. Its initial access methods include phishing, exposed services, and valid account compromise. In 2023, Symantec reported its custom .NET data-enumeration and exfiltration tools.

groups.name: payload
groups.about: Payload emerged in early 2026 and uses Babuk-derived source code to attack Windows and ESXi systems with double extortion. It targets healthcare, energy, real estate, and agriculture. It claimed 12 victims across seven countries within hours of launching its leak site.

groups.name: everest
groups.about: Everest collects and analyzes information about its victims, focusing on customer privacy, financial data, databases, and credit card information. It leaks stolen data on the darknet. It threatens to leak data and keep victims' files if they do not make contact.

groups.name: lockbit5
groups.about: LockBit 5.0, also called ChuongDong, emerged in September 2025 after the February 2024 law enforcement takedown of LockBit. It introduced cross-platform payloads targeting Windows, Linux, and VMware ESXi. It continues the RaaS affiliate model of its predecessors.

groups.name: krybit
groups.about: Krybit is an emerging RaaS group that launched in late March 2026. It offers affiliates an 80/20 revenue split and encrypts Windows, Linux, ESXi, and NAS devices. It became known for a public feud with rival 0APT, with each group leaking the other's operator data.

groups.name: metaencryptor
groups.about: Ransomware group first observed in mid-2023. Targets medium-to-large enterprises in legal, technology, logistics, manufacturing, and finance, mainly in the UK, Europe, and Southeast Asia. Uses AES-256 and RSA-2048 encryption with double extortion.

groups.name: genesis
groups.about: Genesis is an emerging ransomware group first observed in late 2025. It targets small and mid-sized US organizations in healthcare, retail, financial services, legal, and manufacturing. It uses double-extortion tactics, emphasizing data theft and public leaking of stolen data.

Okay, here is the anime-lore update for non-schizo-nerds on AI cybersecurity stuff

Basically AI kind of sucked for awhile, but now we've got pretty good with AI stuff. As a comparison, look at AI generated videos from 2 years ago and compare it to now. It's big brain.

Disclaimer: this isn't doomer posting, read fully if you care, or skip and look at the picture of the cat

Some frameworks, such as the infamous ARTEX, utilizes AI which has been trained on like, 40 years of cybersecurity material. Imagine a human being who could think faster, remember more, and troubleshoot faster, and had all cybersecurity knowledge encapsulated into their little mushy brain

Now imagine this person could work in conjunction with other like minded super schizo nerds and communicate with electricity, instead of words, making communication instantaneous with no way miscommunications.

These super schizo nerds don't need coffee breaks, or smoke breaks, or have meetings, or food, or sleep, friends or family. They can work infinitely with zero breaks.

When you take someone who is educated on offensive cybersecurity ("hacking") and give them something like ARTEX, you've essentially made a regular nerd into a super powered super schizo nerd. Likewise, if you give it to a complete noob, even this dorky noob is suddenly exponentially less nooby.

However, just because attackers have ARTEX, and can work faster, stronger, stinkier, doesn't mean defenders are cooked. Attackers can make mistakes, same as AI-powered attackers. But there is one problem I keep seeing now...

Historically defenders have had issues with budgets, fatigue, burn-out, or apathy from the company, customers, or employees. Suddenly defenders have to face supercharged schizo nerds using AI while the organization they are designated in protecting is understaffed, limited budget, doesn't follow properly security protocols (apathy). It makes defense astronomically more difficult.

Defense has always been hard, but when you're defending an organization and you've got 99 dork attackers, and 1 big brain attackers, it can be challenging. Now you've got 75 big brains (supercharged with AI and anime), and 25 dorks, their job is way, way, way more difficult and stressful.

The problem isn't organizations cannot defend with super mega fuck off AI charged attackers, it's that defenders are constantly chained to budget, executives, or employees. This means companies have to do this thing called "caring" about cybersecurity. This means they have to pay people appropriately, actually do updates, force employees (as much as they can) to care, and follow proper security protocols. If companies do not adapt, they're cooked.

This might be easier for large companies, but for small to medium sized businesses and governments (they're not known for their speed...) are in an extraordinarily difficult position. They either have to find the money in the budget, and care, or face the serious possibility to being obliterated by a stinky nerd super charged with AI. Unfortunately, cybersecurity is expensive. For small to medium sized businesses this places them in a really tough spot.

Anyway, that's my goofy layman talk on AI stuff.

Microsoft FORGE Lab researchers worked with @github and the maintainers of six open-source projects to test whether AI-assisted vulnerability discovery can deliver verified, fixable reports instead of raw findings. https://t.co/4TnBvleVbv 

Codename MDASH, using Microsoft's MAI Cyber model, flagged thousands of possible issues. After triage and manual review, maintainers received 99 private reports, each with a proof of concept and a suggested fix.

The pipeline had three stages:
-MDASH scanned each project and proposed fixes.
-An AI triage agent from GitHub Security Lab removed duplicates, checked validity, and prioritized high-impact bugs. 
-Seven FORGE Lab researchers then validated remaining findings by hand, spending about two days per project.

The projects were AutoGPT, Caddy, Express, FastMCP, ImageMagick, and Netty. Reports went through GitHub private vulnerability reporting, and maintainers decided what to fix and when. The first fixes shipped about a week after the initial scan. 

The research also shows the limits. Manual validation doesn't scale yet, and filtering wasn't perfect: at least one valid report duplicated an issue maintainers already knew about. Each lesson is an opportunity. GitHub and Microsoft will keep working together to help secure open source.

Read the full write-up for the methodology, maintainer feedback, and what's still needed to make AI-assisted vulnerability research work for open source.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence has published a detailed analysis of the phishing campaign exploiting the November 12 Microsoft 365 service disruption, an example of threat actors exploiting notable global incidents in social engineering lures. https://t.co/AnGgiciktm

The campaign uses emails disguised as legitimate Microsoft 365 service-health notifications to target organizations across multiple industry sectors worldwide. Microsoft Defender blocks malicious domains used in this campaign, and Microsoft Defender for Office 365 blocks and quarantines phishing emails.
